title: A changelog the public can read
metaTitle: A changelog people can actually read
excerpt: A public changelog proves the product moves when it is written in the user's language and linked from the product, not buried as commit notes in the footer.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a clear row of things for an article about showing what changed.
caption: A row of garments, each one easy to tell apart. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a public changelog entry say?
faqs.answer: Say what the user can now do, or what they will notice, in their words. Name the date and the area of the product. Leave the ticket number and the internal module name in the repository, and add them only when a technical reader needs them to debug.

faqs.question: Where should the changelog be linked?
faqs.answer: Link it from the product, near the place that changed, and from a stable page people can open later. A footer link alone is easy to miss once someone is inside the tool. A one-line note after a release, with a way to read the rest, is enough.

faqs.question: How often should you publish?
faqs.answer: Publish when a user would notice, not on a quota. A quiet week can stay quiet. A week with three small fixes can be one entry if they belong to the same job. Skipping the page for a month and then dumping raw commits teaches people to ignore it.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Public changelog design is the practice of showing that a product moves, in language a user can read without a tour of the repository. Commit messages prove the code changed. They do not prove the user's week got better.

Put the note where the work is. Link it from the product after a change, not only from a footer item nobody opens once they are inside.

## Write the entry the way a user would notice it

Start from the person's job. "You can export the Friday report without the extra column" is an entry. "Refactor report pipeline" is a note to the team that wrote it. Both can be true. Only one belongs on the public page. If a change has no user-visible effect, it can stay in the commit log.

Use the words already in the product. If the button says Export, the entry says Export. A changelog that invents a new name for the feature forces the reader to translate, and they will not. The same list of twelve object names you use on the marketing site and in the interface should govern this page too. One vocabulary, three surfaces.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether content has a clear purpose and whether a reader can tell who is responsible for it. A changelog's purpose is to tell a user what changed and whether they need to do anything. Sign it with the product's name, or with a person, so it does not read like an anonymous feed. A date on each entry is part of that responsibility. Undated "improvements" feel like a brochure.

Write the sentence a support lead could paste into a reply. If they would have to rewrite it before sending, the entry is still internal. That rewrite is the draft you should have published.

## What a single entry contains

Keep a small shape so the page stays skimmable.

- A date, in the same format every time.
- A plain title that says the change, not the sprint name.
- Two or three sentences on what the user can do now.
- A note if they must act: turn something on, reconnect an account, reread a setting.
- A link to the screen, or to the doc, when the change needs a path.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that describe the page, and it is a good discipline for each entry too. "April updates" describes a calendar. "Export the Friday report without the extra column" describes a change. The page title for the whole changelog can be plain, the product name plus "what changed," so a result in search is not a puzzle. Individual entries can be headings on that page until you have enough to split them.

Say what you removed. Users trust a log that mentions a retired field more than a log that only celebrates additions. If something is broken and you are fixing it, the status page is the better home for the incident. The changelog can record the repair afterward, in a sentence, without turning into a postmortem.

Screenshots help when the interface moved. One crop, with the control visible, beats a gallery. Caption it with the action. Motion, if you show it, needs a still alternative. A looping video of a button is a strange way to say the button moved.

## Link it from the product

The footer of the marketing site is a poor primary home. People who need the changelog are already in the tool, wondering why a screen looks different. Put a quiet link in the product: a "what's new" item in the account menu, or a one-line note on the screen that changed, dismissed once they have seen it.

Do not modal them on every login. A blocking tour for a small copy change trains people to click through without reading, and then they miss the change that mattered. Reserve interruption for something they must do, such as reconnecting an integration. Even then, the interruption should say the action, and the changelog can hold the longer note.

The marketing site can still link to the log. It is proof for a buyer who asks whether the product is maintained. Place that link where a skeptical reader looks: near the product story, not as the last item in a list of legal pages. A buyer comparing you with a tool that ships in public will open it. An empty page, or a page that ends eight months ago, answers the question in the wrong direction.

If you email users about a release, the email and the page should match. One next action in the email. The page holds the record. A campaign of five tips is a different product. The changelog is a record, and records should still be there next month when someone searches.

## How often, and what to skip

Publish when a user would notice. A quiet week can be quiet. Bundling three small fixes into one entry is better than three entries that all say "minor improvements." A quota of one post a week produces filler, and filler teaches people the page is not for them.

Skip internal chores unless they change a promise. A dependency bump the user cannot see does not need a public sentence. A change to how long you keep their data does. A change to who can invite a teammate does. When you are unsure, ask whether support would get a ticket if you stayed silent. If yes, write the entry. If no, leave the commit in the log.

Group by the job, not by the team that shipped it. "Billing" and "invites" are user groups. "Platform squad" is an org chart. Readers do not know your squads, and they should not have to. If two teams shipped on the same day, the page can still read as one product.

Keep a private log if you need one for the board or the investors. Do not make the public page do that job by padding it with momentum language. "Velocity remains high" is not a change. It is a mood. Users came to see the product.

## The page itself

Newest first. Dates visible. Headings that can be scanned in a minute. A reader with a specific worry, "did you change exports," should be able to find the word. A search field is worth adding once the page is longer than a season. Until then, clear headings are the search.

Do not make the page a second marketing homepage. No hero video. No testimonial in the middle of April. The trust comes from the plainness. Type, width, and contrast should match the product's reading surfaces. A changelog in a different brand skin feels unofficial, which is the opposite of the point.

If the product is technical, you can add a short "for developers" line under the user sentence: an endpoint, a field name, a header. Put the user sentence first. Leadly and Trade Moai, as public product interfaces, are reminders that a working screen can be specific without becoming a dump of internals. The changelog should have the same manners. Specific, ordered, no puzzle.

Name the stable URL and keep it stable. People will bookmark it. Support will paste it. Changing the path every redesign breaks those habits. A redirect if you must move it. The title element should stay descriptive across that move, so search results and browser tabs still say what the page is.

## Keeping the page true

Assign an owner. The owner is not "the team." The owner is the person who can publish on the day something ships, or the next morning. If that person is on leave, name the backup in the same note where you name the release owner. A changelog that depends on someone remembering is a changelog that stops.

Write the entry with the change, not two weeks later from memory. The memory will flatter the work and forget the caveat. A caveat is often the sentence the user needed: "this applies to workspaces created after Tuesday," or "existing reports keep the old column until you refresh the template."

Review the page the way you review the product. Read the last five entries aloud. If they could be swapped between any two software companies, they are too vague. If they contain a number you cannot source, take the number out. Invented adoption counts do not make a log more convincing. They make the next true entry harder to trust.

On a Hanabi project the same habit shows up in the client portal: decisions and updates live where the client can find them after the call, not only in a chat scroll. Your users deserve the public version of that habit. A page. A date. A sentence about what changed.

## What the log should not be asked to do

A changelog cannot replace docs. It can point at the new path. It should not be the only place the path is explained. When the change is a new job, write the doc from the job, and let the entry link to it. The next piece, [docs that start from the job](/blog/docs-that-start-from-the-job), is about that structure. Read it when the log is turning into a pile of how-to fragments.

A changelog also cannot carry an incident. During a failure, people need what is affected, what you know, and when you will update. That is a status page. Celebrating the fix in the changelog the next day is fine. Decorating the outage in the changelog while people are stuck is not.

If you want a second pair of eyes on whether your public notes sound like the product, book [an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the last few entries and the screen they refer to. The useful outcome is a shape you can repeat without a writer in the room every Friday.
